beats.content:
Templates are `.html` files in your theme's `templates/` folder, made entirely of block markup. Block markup is an HTML comment that WordPress reads as a block:

```html
<!-- wp:namespace/slug {"align":"full"} /-->
```

- `wp:` tells WordPress this is a block, not an ordinary comment.
- `namespace/slug` names the block. Core blocks drop the `core/` namespace, so the Site Title block is just `<!-- wp:site-title /-->`. Blocks from plugins keep their namespace.
- The JSON after it holds the block's settings.
- A block with nothing inside ends with `/-->`. A block that wraps other blocks has an opening comment and a matching closing comment, such as `<!-- /wp:group -->`.

You rarely type all of this by hand. Build the layout in the Site Editor, open the **Code editor** from the Options (⋮) menu, and copy the markup into your file. Keep everything as blocks: plain HTML that isn't wrapped in block markup shows up as an error in the Site Editor.
beats.question: What does the "wp:" at the start of a comment tell WordPress?

beats.content:
`index.html` is the only template a block theme must have. For each page, WordPress looks for the most specific template your theme has, such as `single.html` for a post, `page.html` for a page or `archive.html` for an archive. If there isn't one, it falls back to `index.html`. Your theme's `templates/index.html` lists posts with a Query Loop block. `"inherit":true` tells the loop to use the query WordPress already ran for the page, so the same template works for the blog, archives and search results: ```html
``` The Group block's `"tagName":"main"` makes it output a `
` element. A `"constrained"` layout keeps its contents to your `contentSize` from theme.json.
beats.goal: See how WordPress picks a template.
beats.question: If your theme only had index.html, which template would a single blog post use?

beats.content:
A template part is a reusable piece of a template, like a header or footer. Parts live directly in your theme's `parts/` folder. Subfolders aren't supported. Your theme already has `parts/header.html`, with the site title and navigation: ```html
``` Unlike templates, parts are never loaded on their own. A template has to include them with the Template Part block: ```html ``` - `slug` is required. WordPress loads `parts/{slug}.html`, so `"header"` loads `parts/header.html`. - `tagName` sets the wrapping element, here `
`. You can also register parts in theme.json under the top-level `templateParts` key, with `name` (the file name without `.html`), `title` and `area`. WordPress 7.x has four built-in areas: `header`, `footer`, `uncategorized` (shown as "General") and `navigation-overlay` (shown as "Navigation Overlay", new in 7.0). Registering is optional, but it gives the part a proper label in the Site Editor.
beats.goal: Reuse a header with a template part.
beats.question: Why put the header in a part instead of copying it into every template?

beats.content:
When you, or anyone using your theme, edits a template or part in the Site Editor and saves, the change is stored in the site's database. That saved copy then takes priority over the file in your theme.

This is great for site owners, but it means the theme files don't change. To ship your design, the markup has to end up back in the theme's `templates/` and `parts/` files. You can copy it from the Code editor, or use the Create Block Theme plugin, covered in the last lesson.
beats.goal: Know where Site Editor changes go.
beats.question: You edited the header in the Site Editor and saved. Has parts/header.html changed?
